about: Plain-language meanings for every name in the runtime's performance file. Read by perf-report.ts (each row's `extra`), checked by perf-report.test.ts, and listed in docs/perf-glossary.md. Span and count keys are the row-name form of the runtime's probe names (lower case, dashes for colons and spaces); a family matches by start and end of that form, with {name} the part between.

floor.says: The same input as a fresh import, loaded plainly into one SQLite file, to read a fresh import against. It is not a lower bound.
floor.total: The same input a fresh import takes in, loaded plainly into SQLite: read and decompress the Bundle, parse it, flatten each resource to one row of a table named for its resource type (a plain value is a column, anything nested is kept as its JSON text) and insert every row into a SQLite file in one transaction, with the SQLite the runtime uses and none of its settings changed. Only the insert is SQL; reading, parsing and flattening are JavaScript. Nested values are kept as JSON text with no further tables, and SQLite's default journal and synchronous settings are kept. It does no mapping to the Cascade vocabulary, keeps no provenance, does no matching of records that are the same, builds no derived views and writes no files, and a faster load of the same input could exist, so it is not a lower bound. The encrypted import is compared with this same unencrypted load. It says what loading costs, not what the import's other work adds up to; the pages do not split the difference beyond the stages the flame graphs measure.

measures.total: The headline: the whole scenario from start to finish, the median of the runs.
measures.import: Importing the whole record into the pod.
measures.first-screen: Asking the questions the first screen shows.
measures.first-read: The first question asked of the reopened pod ('My active conditions').
measures.second-read: A second question asked of the reopened pod ('My active medications').
measures.close: Closing the pod, saving its database.
measures.parse: Floor stage: reading the compressed Bundle, decompressing it and parsing the JSON. A fresh import parses the Bundle too: the harness reads, decompresses and parses it once before the import's clock starts, but the import is handed the Bundle's bytes and, from reading its code, parses them again inside its own time (not traced). So this stage and the import's own parsing are about the same work, with this stage also counting reading and decompressing, which the import's clock does not.
measures.flatten: Floor stage: turning each parsed resource into one row of the table for its resource type, plain values as columns and anything nested as its JSON text.
measures.insert: Floor stage: creating a table for each resource type and inserting every row in one transaction into a SQLite file on disk, then closing the file.
measures.rss: Memory the process was holding when the scenario's work was done, in bytes: after the first screen and before closing for a new pod, after the second read for a reopened one, after a first read and before the pages for the question pages.
measures.peak-rss: The most memory the process held at any moment, in bytes.
measures.probed-total: The scenario's time in one run with the probe on, which slows some work; its stages are from this run and are for finding where time goes, never for adding up to the headline.
measures.phase-loading-the-adapter: Import part: loading the adapter that knows this kind of record.
measures.phase-converting: Import part: converting the source record into the pod's own format.
measures.phase-saving: Import part: writing the converted records into the pod.
measures.phase-judging: Import part: claiming, as the pod's owner, the profiles the person confirmed are theirs.

selfRows: Own time: the time some call of it was in progress with none of the spans inside it in progress, that is the time spent in its own code, or waiting. Unlike its stage time it leaves out what the spans inside it took, so the largest own times are the places to look first.
runs: Each build also keeps a trace of its probed run ("Where the time went": every call with its start, end and the call it ran inside, drawn as a flame graph) and a CPU profile of an unprobed run ("Which code took it": every function the processor was sampled in), both opened in speedscope. The builds are listed at https://jayostis.github.io/cascade-runtime-js/perf/runs/, newest first, with the files each still has: traces for the newest 30 builds, CPU profiles for the newest 5, and the large size's files for the newest 7 builds that ran it. A trace draws each call under the call that ran it, side by side where calls ran at the same time; where more than 32 calls of one step ran at once, they are drawn as one merged bar for each stretch of time some of them were running, labelled with how many (for example "files.encrypt × 40 at once"), so no time is left out of the picture. The Bridge says how long each of its queries took in all and not when it ran, so a trace does not draw them: the index lists, for each build, the time per Bridge query, positions unknown, and a Bridge stage's own time includes the queries it ran.
